title: Find the Duplicate Number
description: Brute force to optimized: a hash map count versus Floyd's cycle detection applied to the array reframed as an implicit linked structure.

blocks.text: Given an array of integers nums containing n + 1 integers, where each integer is in the range [1, n] inclusive, there is exactly one repeated number in nums (though it may appear more than twice). Find and return this repeated number, WITHOUT modifying the array, and using only O(1) extra space.

blocks.caption: Treating each index as a node and nums[index] as its "next pointer" turns this array problem into a linked-list cycle detection problem

blocks.text: Since every value in the array is itself a valid index (1 to n), the array can be reinterpreted as a linked structure: starting at index 0, "follow" to index nums[0], then to index nums[nums[0]], and so on. Because the duplicate value causes TWO different indices to both point to the SAME next index, this implicit structure is guaranteed to contain a cycle, and the duplicate value is exactly the cycle's entry point.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Game of "Follow the Number" That Must Loop
blocks.text: Imagine standing at position 0, and the rule is "look at the number written there, then walk to THAT position number." Since there are only n possible positions to walk to but n+1 numbers guaranteeing a repeat, this walk is mathematically guaranteed to eventually revisit some position it has already been to, forming a loop. The single repeated NUMBER in the array is exactly the position where two different paths converge into that loop, which is precisely the loop's entrance.

blocks.caption: The duplicate value is the ONLY value referenced by more than one index, so it must be exactly where the implicit "list" cycles back on itself

blocks.text: Before reaching for a hash set or frequency map (which would use O(n) extra space, violating the constraint), notice that treating array VALUES as INDICES turns this into a disguised linked-list cycle detection problem, exactly like Linked List Cycle II.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since every value is a valid index (1 to n) and there are n+1 values, by the pigeonhole principle, at least one value MUST repeat.

Observation 2: Defining "next(i) = nums[i]" turns the array into an implicit functional graph (each index points to exactly one other index), and the guaranteed repeat means this graph MUST contain a cycle.

Observation 3: The duplicate value is special: it is the ONLY value pointed to by two DIFFERENT indices (since it appears more than once in the array), which is EXACTLY the defining property of a cycle's entrance node.

Observation 4: This means Floyd's cycle detection (slow/fast pointers, then the two-phase find-the-entrance technique), the exact same algorithm as Linked List Cycle II, can be applied directly, using array indexing as the "next" operation instead of following actual pointers.

Recognizing this problem as "Linked List Cycle II in disguise" is the single biggest insight required here.
This is Floyd's cycle detection (identical in structure to Linked List Cycle II), applied to the implicit linked structure formed by treating array values as indices.
Use a hash map to count occurrences of every value; the very first value whose count exceeds 1 is the duplicate.

items: Walk through the array, incrementing a count for each value in a hash map.
The moment any value's count exceeds 1, that value is confirmed as the duplicate and can be returned immediately.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A hash map directly counts occurrences regardless of the array's specific value range, generalizing beyond this problem's specific [1, n] constraint.
Returning immediately upon detecting a count exceeding 1 avoids unnecessary further scanning once the answer is already known.

blocks.text: Correctly identifies the duplicate value, since a hash map directly and reliably tracks occurrence counts.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single linear pass.
Space: O(n), for the hash map.
Limitation: the O(n) extra space directly violates this problem's O(1) space requirement; Floyd's cycle detection achieves the same result using only a few integer variables.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force needs O(n) space for a hash map. Instead, recognize that treating "nums[i]" as "the next index to visit" turns the array into an implicit linked structure guaranteed to contain a cycle (by the pigeonhole principle), with the duplicate value as exactly its entrance. Apply Floyd's two-phase cycle detection (identical to Linked List Cycle II) directly on this implicit structure.

Phase 1: initialize slow = nums[0], fast = nums[nums[0]]; advance slow by nums[slow] and fast by nums[nums[fast]] until they meet (confirming a cycle). Phase 2: reset one pointer to index 0 (representing the true starting point); advance both remaining pointers by nums[pointer] (same speed) until they meet again; that meeting point is the duplicate value.
Apply Floyd's two-phase cycle detection directly on the array, treating nums[i] as the "next" index/value.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Both pointers converge at value 2, the correct duplicate, matching the expected result.

codes.python:
def find_duplicate(nums):
    slow = nums[0]                                                          # phase 1: detect the cycle (treating index -> nums[index] as "next")
    fast = nums[nums[0]]
    while slow != fast:
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[nums[fast]]

    ptr1 = 0                                                                 # phase 2: locate the cycle's entrance (same trick as Linked List Cycle II)
    ptr2 = slow
    while ptr1 != ptr2:
        ptr1 = nums[ptr1]
        ptr2 = nums[ptr2]
    return ptr1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(find_duplicate([1, 3, 4, 2, 2]))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), both phases together still take a bounded number of linear steps.
Space: O(1) extra, only a few integer variables are used.

The exact same mathematical proof from Linked List Cycle II applies here: after slow and fast meet, resetting one pointer to the TRUE start (index 0 in this array version) and advancing both remaining pointers at equal speed guarantees they meet again exactly at the cycle's entrance, which corresponds precisely to the duplicate value in this array framing.

items: slow and fast are initialized one step ahead (using nums[0] and nums[nums[0]]) rather than both starting exactly at index 0, purely to allow a clean while-loop condition instead of a do-while.
Phase 2 resets one pointer to TRUE index 0 (not a node value), representing the conceptual starting point of the "walk," exactly mirroring Linked List Cycle II's dummy-head reset.
No node objects are created at all; every step is just an array index lookup, making this a very lightweight application of the technique.

blocks.text: When an array's values are themselves valid indices into that same array, it can often be reframed as an implicit linked structure; if a repeat is guaranteed (pigeonhole principle), Floyd's cycle detection technique applies directly, achieving O(1) space where a hash-based approach would need O(n).

items: Attempting to sort the array or use binary search on the VALUE range without first recognizing the more elegant cycle-detection reframing (a valid alternative, but more complex to reason about correctly).
Forgetting that phase 2 must reset to TRUE index 0, not to nums[0] or some other value, when locating the cycle's entrance.
Modifying the array in place (for example, via negation-marking) when the problem explicitly disallows it.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Array values are all valid INDICES into the same array, with a guaranteed duplicate, and O(1) space is required" points toward reframing the array as an implicit linked list and applying Floyd's cycle detection.

items: Why is a cycle GUARANTEED to exist here? By the pigeonhole principle: n+1 values, each restricted to [1, n], forces at least one repeat, which creates a node with two incoming "pointers," the hallmark of a cycle.

Could binary search on the value range also solve this? Yes: count how many values are <= mid for each candidate mid, and binary search using that count to narrow down the duplicate, achieving O(n log n) time but WITHOUT modifying the array or needing extra space beyond O(1), as an alternative approach.

How does this problem's technique relate to Linked List Cycle II? It is the mathematically identical algorithm, applied to an implicit "next" relationship (array indexing) instead of literal linked-list pointers.

A direct reapplication of Linked List Cycle II's two-phase Floyd's algorithm, reframed onto an array via the "value as index" trick, demonstrating that this technique generalizes beyond literal linked structures.

blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (Floyd's cycle detection on the implicit structure): O(n) time, O(1) space.
